title: Anarchy
subtitle: Why great powers can never quite trust each other

lines: Imagine a neighbourhood with no police.
No courts. No one to call if someone breaks down your door.
Every house must guard itself. And every house knows it.
This is not a thought experiment. It is the world stage. And it has been, for almost four hundred years.
In 1648, after thirty years of war had emptied whole regions of Germany, the rulers of Europe signed a peace in Westphalia.
It settled borders. But it also settled something deeper.
There would be no emperor above them. No higher authority. Each state would be sovereign, and alone.
Political scientists have a word for that arrangement. Not chaos. Anarchy.
Simply, the absence of a ruler.
Anarchy sets a trap.
Suppose one state builds walls to feel safe.
Its neighbour cannot know whether those walls are for defence, or for the next war.
So it builds walls too. And now the first state feels less safe than before.
In 1978, Robert Jervis gave this a name. The security dilemma.
Every step toward safety makes everyone a little more afraid.
So states watch the scales.
When one power grows too strong, the others tend to band together against it.
Napoleon learned this. So did the Kaiser.
Kenneth Waltz called it the balance of power, and argued that it forms almost automatically, whether anyone intends it or not.
Then, in 1945, the stakes changed.
A war between great powers could now end them all.
Thomas Schelling saw that the bomb turned war into a contest of nerves. Not who is stronger, but who is more willing to risk the unthinkable.
The Doomsday Clock has stood near midnight ever since.
No one designed this system. No one can leave it.
Every state is still a house with no one to call.
The question has never been whether they will compete.
Only whether they can compete, without destroying each other.
